name: PulsePoint MoodGlyph Affective Display Implant
body_location: subdermal forehead — thin bioluminescent display lattice beneath the skin of the upper forehead
description:
The MoodGlyph is a subdermal bioluminescent display panel implanted just beneath the epidermis of the forehead, spanning roughly 6cm by 3cm. It renders programmable glyphs, color gradients, and abstract animations that shift in response to either biometric emotional data — heart rate variability, galvanic skin response, cortisol proxy signals — or manual overrides set through a paired app. The display is subtle in bright daylight but clearly visible in dim environments, producing soft light through the skin rather than projecting outward. PulsePoint's proprietary EmoteOS library includes over 400 pre-designed glyph sets ranging from minimalist geometric pulses to elaborate animated iconography. Users can design custom glyph sets or purchase community packs through the PulsePoint social marketplace. The display does not emit UV or harmful radiation; it is powered by the same thermoelectric passive cell used across PulsePoint's product line.

The MoodGlyph began as a niche youth fashion item in Tier 2 neighborhoods in the early 2180s and has since exploded into one of the most visible social cyberware implants in GLMZ. It is particularly popular among teenagers and people in their twenties, who use it as both genuine emotional expression and deliberate aesthetic identity — choosing glyph sets the way previous generations chose tattoos or hairstyles. For neurodivergent users who struggle with facial expression regulation, the MoodGlyph offers a reliable secondary channel for communicating emotional state without requiring voluntary facial control. Therapy clinics have begun prescribing specific glyph-set protocols for patients with flat affect disorders. At parties, in clubs, and on transit, a room full of MoodGlyph users produces a quiet, shifting light show that many describe as one of the most distinctly GLMZ aesthetic experiences.
installation_requirements: Outpatient clinic or licensed kiosk; 30-minute procedure under topical anesthetic; no recovery time required
maintenance: EmoteOS firmware updates quarterly; annual brightness calibration; display panel rated for 15 years before requiring replacement
side_effects: Mild forehead tenderness and visible bruising for 3–5 days post-installation
Occasional involuntary glyph flicker during REM sleep if biometric mode is left active
Some users report initial self-consciousness about involuntary emotional readouts before learning to use manual override mode
Rare cases of minor skin luminosity unevenness at display edges, typically resolving within 6 weeks
cultural_context: The MoodGlyph is simultaneously a fashion statement, a social signal, and a minor class marker. On the Gray Zone and in Tier 2 neighborhoods, the glyph sets someone chooses are read as carefully as clothing — certain glyph aesthetics are associated with specific subcultures, neighborhoods, and social factions. In Tier 3 corporate environments, wearing a MoodGlyph to work is still considered slightly informal, and many users switch to a neutral 'professional mode' glyph — a slow, barely visible pulse — during business hours. Tier 4 and above users rarely have them at all, considering them gauche, though some Tier 4 youth adopt them ironically. There is an ongoing low-level social debate about consent and emotional transparency — critics argue that biometric-linked MoodGlyphs constitute a form of involuntary emotional disclosure in social settings, while proponents argue it has made human interaction more honest and less exhausting.
known_users: Teenagers and young adults across Tier 1–3 as a primary fashion and identity accessory
Neurodivergent individuals using it as a therapeutic communication aid
Artists and performers who integrate glyph displays into their aesthetic work
Social workers and counselors who use neutral therapeutic glyph sets to signal approachability
Club and music scene regulars who invest in elaborate custom animation packs
story_hooks: A series of MoodGlyph units in a the Gray Zone neighborhood have been remotely hijacked to display a specific glyph — an unfamiliar symbol no one recognizes — simultaneously at 3am. It happens three nights running. Then one of the users goes missing.

A corporate negotiation goes sideways when one party realizes the other's lead negotiator has their MoodGlyph in full biometric mode — every stress response and moment of deception has been silently broadcast across the table for the entire meeting.

A PulsePoint glyph pack sold through the community marketplace contains a hidden subroutine that maps and transmits the emotional biometric data of every user who downloads it. Someone needs to find out who built it and why.
